questiontext.text: Which line lights bit k of x without changing any other bit?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. OR with a mask that has a single lit bit forces that bit to 1 and leaves every other bit alone. Plain assignment would erase all the other bits.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 13;
x |= 2;
x &= ~8;
x ^= 1;
cout << x << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 13 is 1101. Setting bit 1 gives 1111 (15). Clearing bit 3 gives 0111 (7). Flipping bit 0 gives 0110, which is 6.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this code print?

main.cpp
cout << (3 << 4) << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A left shift by 4 doubles the number four times, which means multiplying by 16. The number 3 is 11, which becomes 110000, that is 3 x 16 = 48.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 6;
cout << (x << 2) << " " << (x >> 1) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 6 is 110. Shifting left by 2 gives 11000, which is 24. Shifting right by 1 gives 11, which is 3. The program prints 24 3.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What does x &= (1 << k); do?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The mask 1 << k has a 1 only at bit k. The operator & keeps a bit only where the mask is 1, so every other bit becomes 0. To clear bit k we need the inverted mask: x &= ~(1 << k);.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: It keeps bit k alone and clears all the other bits

name.text: Q06 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operator into the gap so the program prints 8.

main.cpp
int x = 12;
x [[1]] (1 << 2);
cout << x << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. 12 is 1100 and 1 << 2 is 0100. The operator ^= flips bit 2, which was lit, so it goes off and the result is 1000, that is 8. With |= nothing changes (12), and with &= only bit 2 is kept (4).

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 12;
x ^= (1 << 2);
cout << x << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 10;
for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
    cout << ((x >> k) & 1);
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 10 is 1010. The loop reads bit 0, then bit 1, then bit 2, then bit 3, so it prints the bits from the lowest to the highest: 0101.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: How do we get the value of bit k as exactly 0 or 1?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The shift x >> k moves bit k to the far right, and & 1 keeps that bit alone, so we get exactly 0 or 1. The expression x & (1 << k) gives 0 or the mask value 2^k, which is not always 1.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 3.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. x must exist first. Flipping bit 1 turns 11 into 01, and then setting bit 1 brings it back to 11, which is 3. In the opposite order, setting does nothing and flipping then gives 1.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 3;
x ^= (1 << 1);
x |= (1 << 1);
cout << x << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with its purpose.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

(x >> k) & 1  →  [[1]]

x |= (1 << k)  →  [[2]]

x &= ~(1 << k)  →  [[3]]

x ^= (1 << k)  →  [[4]]

x << k  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Each task is a single expression built from a shift, a mask and one bitwise operator. Learn these five and you can read most bit-manipulation code.

The correct answer:

  • (x >> k) & 1 → Reads bit k as 0 or 1
  • x |= (1 << k) → Lights bit k
  • x &= ~(1 << k) → Switches bit k off
  • x ^= (1 << k) → Flips bit k
  • x << k → Multiplies x by 2^k

questiontext.text: Which line switches bit k off without changing any other bit?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. ~(1 << k) has a 0 at bit k and 1 everywhere else, so & clears that bit and keeps all the others.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 0;
x |= (1 << 3);
x |= (1 << 0);
x ^= (1 << 3);
cout << x << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. We start from 0. Setting bit 3 gives 1000 (8). Setting bit 0 gives 1001 (9). Flipping bit 3 switches it off again, leaving 0001, which is 1.

questiontext.text:
Sort each expression: does it change x, or only read it?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

x |= 4;  →  [[1]]

x &= ~1;  →  [[1]]

x ^= 1;  →  [[1]]

(x >> 2) & 1  →  [[2]]

x << 1  →  [[2]]

x & (1 << 3)  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Compound assignments such as |=, &= and ^= modify x. The other expressions only compute a value from x and leave it untouched; even x << 1 does not change x unless we write x <<= 1.

The correct answer:

Changes x: x |= 4;, x &= ~1;, x ^= 1;
Only reads x: (x >> 2) & 1, x << 1, x & (1 << 3)

questiontext.text:
What does this code print?

main.cpp
cout << (13 & (1 << 3)) << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 13 is 1101, and 1 << 3 is 1000. Their AND is 1000, which is 8 and not 1. This is why x & (1 << k) should be used as a condition, not as a 0-or-1 value.

What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4;
int p = READ | WRITE;
p &= ~READ;
p |= EXEC;
cout << p << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. READ | WRITE is 3 (011). Removing READ leaves 010. Adding EXEC gives 110, which is 6.

name.text: Q16 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operators into the gaps so the program prints 5.

main.cpp
int x = 15;
x [[1]] ~(1 << 1);
x [[2]] (1 << 3);
cout << x << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. 15 is 1111. &= ~(1 << 1) clears bit 1 and gives 1101 (13). ^= (1 << 3) then flips bit 3 and gives 0101, which is 5. Using |= would not clear or flip anything.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 15;
x &= ~(1 << 1);
x ^= (1 << 3);
cout << x << endl;

questiontext.text: Which expression builds a mask with only bit 40 lit?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A plain 1 is an int with only 32 bits, so shifting it by 40 is wrong. Writing 1LL makes it a 64-bit number, which has room for bit 40.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps that switch off bit k of a number x.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. First we build the mask with a single lit bit, then we invert it so that only bit k is 0, then we combine it with x using AND so that bit k goes off, and finally we store the result.

The correct answer:

  1. Build the mask 1 << k
  2. Invert the mask with ~
  3. Combine x with the inverted mask using &
  4. Store the result back into x

questiontext.text:
Match each word with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Mask  →  [[1]]

Shift left  →  [[2]]

Shift right  →  [[3]]

Toggle  →  [[4]]

Bit index  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These are the words you will hear whenever people talk about bit tricks.

The correct answer:

  • Mask → A number built to select particular bits
  • Shift left → Moves every bit toward the high end, multiplying the number
  • Shift right → Moves every bit toward the low end, dropping the remainder
  • Toggle → Turning a bit into its opposite
  • Bit index → The position of a bit, counted from 0 at the right

questiontext.text:
Sort each task by the line that does it.

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Turn a lamp on  →  [[1]]

Grant a permission  →  [[1]]

Turn a lamp off  →  [[2]]

Revoke a permission  →  [[2]]

Enable a feature flag  →  [[1]]

Clear an error flag  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Setting a bit uses OR with the mask. Clearing a bit uses AND with the inverted mask. Granting and enabling are "set" operations; revoking and clearing are "clear" operations.

The correct answer:

x |= mask: Turn a lamp on, Grant a permission, Enable a feature flag
x &= ~mask: Turn a lamp off, Revoke a permission, Clear an error flag
